Renormalization in Combinatorially Non-Local Field Theories: the BPHZ Momentum Scheme This paper is a contribution to the Special Issue on Algebraic Structures in Perturbative Quantum Field Theory in honor of Dirk Kreimer for his 60th birthday. The full collection is available at https://www.emis.de/journals/SIGMA/Kreimer.html
Johannes THÜRIGEN ab

Abstract
Various combinatorially non-local field theories are known to be renormalizable. Still, explicit calculations of amplitudes are very rare and restricted to matrix field theory. In this contribution I want to demonstrate how the BPHZ momentum scheme in terms of the Connes–Kreimer Hopf algebra applies to any combinatorially non-local field theory which is renormalizable. This algebraic method improves the understanding of known results in noncommutative field theory in its matrix formulation. Furthermore, I use it to provide new explicit perturbative calculations of amplitudes in tensorial field theories of rank r > 2 r>2 .



keywords
non-local field theory; renormalization; Hopf algebras; multiple polylogarithms

1
Introduction

Since Dirk Kreimer’s seminal work
[
29
]
it is well known that a Hopf algebra of divergent Feynman diagrams is the universal structure underlying renormalization in perturbative quantum field theory
[
16
,
17
,
30
]
.
A classical example is BPHZ momentum subtraction as used for the general proof of renormalization
[
7
,
27
,
55
]
.
In
[
53
]
I have shown that the Connes–Kreimer Hopf algebra describes renormalization not only in field theories with point-like interactions but also with full generality in combinatorially non-local field theories (cNLFT) such as non-commutative and matrix field theory
[
23
,
28
,
54
]
, tensorial field theories
[
2
,
3
]
and group field theory
[
13
,
20
,
37
]
.

So far, explicit calculations of renormalized amplitudes in cNLFT depending on external kinematic variables are only known for noncommutative field theory and its matrix-field representation using the BPHZ momentum scheme
[
6
,
22
,
28
]
.
In fact, exact solutions for matrix field theory have been found recently
[
11
,
21
,
41
]
and the perturbative results are mainly used as a check of consistency
[
22
,
28
]
.
For other examples of cNLFT, renormalizability has been proven for various field theories with tensorial interactions
[
2
,
3
,
4
,
13
,
14
,
15
]
but no explicit results of amplitudes, let alone of full renormalized correlation functions, are known.
1
1

1

Exact solutions similar to matrix field theory
[
41
]
have been found for a super-renormalizable rank-3 tensor field in
[
42
]
; due to the restriction to a single tensorial interaction and renormalization even of convergent amplitudes, a closer look reveals that this is still the mentioned matrix theory in disguise.
Using the Hopf-algebraic structure of renormalization here I will give new results for explicit amplitudes of perturbative tensorial field theory.

Explicit perturbative calculations in matrix field theory use a version of Zimmermann’s forest formula
[
55
]
adapted to ribbon graphs
[
22
]
.
While agreement with exact non-perturbative solutions shows that this implementation of the BPHZ momentum scheme is perfectly valid, it uses a very peculiar definition of subdiagrams which are not themselves ribbon graphs, thus strictly speaking in a different class of diagrams.
Here I will show how BPHZ momentum subtraction can be defined on any cNLFT in Kreimer’s way using the Hopf algebra of divergent diagrams and a subtraction operator as a Taylor expansion
which is a Rota–Baxter operator on the algebra of amplitudes.
This gives two results:
First, it reproduces in a very natural way the known perturbative calculations in matrix field theory
[
22
,
28
]
.
Second, it provides the algorithm to calculate renormalized amplitudes in any cNLFT in a straightforward way.
I will demonstrate this for the example of tadpole and sunrise diagrams in field theory with tensor-invariant interactions.

The physical meaning of amplitudes in cNLFT is not as obvious as for scattering events of high energy particles described by standard-model quantum field theories.
Matrix field theory can be understood as a representation of field theory of elementary particles on non-commutative (Moyal-deformed) spacetime which still allows for such scattering interpretation.
On the other hand, one main application of theories with tensor fields of higher rank
r>2
are models of quantum gravity as their perturbative series is a sum over
r
-dimensional combinatorial (pseudo) manifolds
[
24
]
and one can build models which have gravitational amplitudes on such discrete manifolds as lattice gauge theories
[
13
,
20
,
37
]
, known as spin foam models
[
43
]
.
Then, the main challenge is to recover continuous
D=4
dimensional spacetime in some critical regime of the theory
[
38
,
46
]
in the sense of continuous random geometries
[
1
,
33
,
36
]
;
to this end, non-perturbative results like
[
44
]
are necessary.
However, also perturbation theory might be the right starting point towards this goal, either by identification of appropriate linear combinations of amplitudes in the perturbative series related to non-perturbative structures as found for example via topological recursion
[
10
,
11
]
or exploiting the Hopf-algebraic structure of perturbative renormalization leading to Kreimer’s combinatorial Dyson–Schwinger equations
[
5
,
12
,
31
,
32
]
.
Thus, the explicit perturbative results presented here might also be seen as a starting point to investigate the non-perturbative regime of cNLFT.

2
Feynman rules in cNLFT

In the following I introduce the general structure of renormalization as captured by a Hopf algebra
[
29
,
30
]
.
In parallel, I explain its application to combinatorially non-local field theory.
This is largely based on
[
53
]
where one can find the precise details of combinatorial and algebraic definitions and statements.
Here, the emphasis is on the practical use for perturbative calculations in field theory.

A perturbative expansion in coupling constants is a formal power series labelled by Feynman diagrams.
Feynman rules associate to each diagram
\Gamma
an amplitude
A_{\Gamma}
, i.e., the coefficient in this power series.
This can be understood as a map from diagrams to amplitudes

\displaystyle A\colon\ \mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{A},\qquad\Gamma\mapsto A(\Gamma)=A_{\Gamma}.

In the perturbative series these amplitudes are summed and
for renormalization it will also be necessary to multiply them which demands an algebra
\mathcal{A}
of amplitudes.
This structure is mirrored in a
\mathbb{Q}
-algebra
\mathcal{G}
generated by the set of diagrams in which multiplication is simply the disjoint union of diagrams,
m_{\mathcal{G}}(\Gamma_{1}\otimes\Gamma_{2}):=\Gamma_{1}\sqcup\Gamma_{2}
.
Both algebras are unital with unit
u_{\mathcal{G}}\colon\mathbb{Q}\to\mathcal{G},q\mapsto q\mathbbm{1}
where
\mathbbm{1}\in\mathcal{G}
is the empty diagram and
u_{\mathcal{A}}
maps to the amplitude
A(\mathbbm{1})=1
.
The map
A
must then be an algebra homomorphism.

A combinatorially non-local field theory (cNLFT) is characterized by a pairing of arguments at interaction vertices which leads to strand graphs as Feynman diagrams (called
2
-graphs
in
[
53
]
2
2

2

I thank an unknown referee for pointing out the possible confusions with the notion of a “two-graph” as defined by G. Higman
[
48
,
51
]
. For this reason I will here use “strand graph” for what is defined as “2-graph” in
[
53
]
.
).
That is, order-
n
interactions are of the form

\displaystyle S_{\textsc{ia}}[\Phi]=\lambda_{\gamma}\int\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{p}_{i}\prod_{(ia,jb)}\delta\big(p_{i}^{a}-p_{j}^{b}\big)\prod_{i=1}^{n}{\Phi}(\boldsymbol{p}_{i}),

(2.1)

where the field
\Phi
depends on
r
arguments
\boldsymbol{p}=\big(p^{1},\dots,p^{r}\big)
of which each
p^{a}
is in a
d
-dimensional manifold. For simplicity I will consider
p^{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}
throughout this paper.
The product over pairs
(ia,jb)
means that for each argument
p_{i}^{a}
there is a convolution in terms of the Dirac distribution
\delta\big(p_{i}^{a}-p_{j}^{b}\big)
with exactly one other argument
p_{j}^{b}
.
Diagrammatically, these convolutions cannot be fully captured by a vertex in a graph but it is necessary to add a second layer called strands.
For example,

is the diagrammatic representation of an interaction vertex of
n=4
fields (red) with
r=3
arguments each (green) which are convoluted pairwise (blue dots); this is equivalent to, on the right-hand side of the equation,
a vertex (black) with half-edges (red) and additional edges (green) adjacent to these half-edges which characterize the interaction vertex by a graph.
Thus, interactions are labelled in general by
vertex graphs

\gamma
and so are their coupling constants
\lambda_{\gamma}
.
A set of graphs
\mathbf{G}_{1}^{v}
determines the diagrammatics of a given theory.

Feynman diagrams follow as usual by Wick contraction of the fields according to a quadratic Gaussian part of the action.
The arguments
p^{a}
of the field
\Phi
are not necessarily ordered, i.e., the quadratic part
might pair the
r
arguments according to an arbitrary permutation
{\sigma_{2}}
,
3
3

3

Note that for a given permutation this quadratic form might not be positive which, however, is necessary to yield a Gaussian measure. With the sum
\sum_{{\sigma_{2}}}
over an appropriate set of such permutations
{\sigma_{2}}
the quadratic form becomes positive and thus Gaussian. I thank one of the referees for pointing this out.

\displaystyle S_{0}(\Phi)=\frac{1}{2}\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{p}_{i}\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{p}_{j}\Phi(\boldsymbol{p}_{i})\sum_{{\sigma_{2}}}{\prod_{a=1}^{r}\delta\big(p_{i}^{a}-p_{j}^{{\sigma_{2}}(a)}\big)}\bigg({\sum_{a=1}^{r}|p_{i}^{a}|^{2\zeta}+\mu}\bigg)\Phi(\boldsymbol{p}_{j}),

(2.2)

where
\mu
is a mass parameter and the scaling
{2\zeta}
of the propagator is in general parametrized by a
\zeta>0
, usually
\zeta\in{}]0,1]
.
This leads to the general class of strand graphs defined in
[
53
]
under the name of “2-graphs” and based on
[
39
,
52
]
.
Still, in many theories this permutation is fixed. For example, in Hermitian matrix field theory
[
28
,
54
]
, the strand graphs are combinatorial maps (ribbon graphs ) and
{\sigma_{2}}
is fixed by the orientation of the vertices, e.g., in

(2.3)

the pairing of strands adjacent to half edges
i\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}
along the edges
\{1,2\}
,
\{3,5\}
and
\{4,6\}
is determined by the orientation of the vertices
(1)
,
(234)
and
(576)
(see Fig. 2 in
[
53
]
for further details).
Following a strand through the strand graph defines a face which is an internal face if the strand is closed and external otherwise.
In the example
\Gamma
there is one internal face
(3564)
and one external face
(764212357)
.
The external structure of a strand graph
\Gamma
is the vertex graph
\gamma
obtained by deleting all internal edges and internal faces which is the boundary
\gamma=\partial\Gamma
.

The above Gaussian and interaction parts of the action, equations (
2.2
) and (
2.1
), lead to an identification of variables
p^{a}
along strands and thus to the following Feynman rules:
For a strand graph
\Gamma
, the amputated amplitude
A_{\Gamma}
is an integral consisting of

1)

a Lebesgue integral
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathrm{d}q_{f}
for each internal face
f\in\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{int}}_{\Gamma}
, integrating over the variable identifying
q_{f}=p_{i}^{a}
for all strands
a
at half edges
i
along
f
,

2)

a propagator factor
\frac{1}{\sum_{a=1}^{r}|p_{i}^{a}|^{2\zeta}+\mu}
for each internal edge
e=\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\Gamma}
,

3)

a coupling constant
\lambda_{\gamma_{v}}
for each vertex
v\in\mathcal{V}_{\Gamma}
with vertex graph
\gamma=\gamma_{v}
and

These rules define the algebra homomorphism
A\colon\mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{A}
to the algebra
\mathcal{A}
of (formal) integral functions with rational functions as integrands,

\displaystyle A_{\Gamma}\colon\ \{p_{f}\}_{f\in\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\Gamma}}\mapsto A_{\Gamma}(\{p_{f}\}):=\prod_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\Gamma}}\lambda_{\gamma_{v}}\prod_{f\in\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{int}}_{\Gamma}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathrm{d}q_{f}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}_{\Gamma}}\frac{1}{\sum_{a=1}^{r}|p_{i}^{a}|^{2\zeta}+\mu}.

They depend on external variables
p_{f}
for each external face
f\in\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\Gamma}
adjacent to
at least one internal edge
, given again by identifying
p_{f}=p^{a}_{i}
for all half edges
i
and adjacent strands
a
along
f
.
Importantly, only faces in this subset
\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}}\subset\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{ext}}
of external faces play a role: If a face is not adjacent to any internal edge, there is no propagator in which the corresponding variable occurs and the amputated amplitude
A_{\Gamma}
does not depend on it. This is in contrast to local field theory where loop amplitudes always depend on all external variables.

Multiplication in the algebra
\mathcal{A}
of amplitudes is given by multiplication of integrands.
That is, the product of two amplitudes
A,B\in\mathcal{A}
with

\displaystyle A(p_{1},\dots,p_{m})=c_{A}\int\prod_{i}\mathrm{d}q_{i}I_{A}(p_{1},\dots,p_{m},q_{1},\dots,q_{k})

and

\displaystyle B(r_{1},\dots,r_{n})=c_{B}\int\prod_{j}\mathrm{d}s_{j}I_{B}(r_{1},\dots,r_{n},s_{1},\dots,s_{l}),

where the integrands
I_{A}
and
I_{B}
are rational functions is

\displaystyle(A\cdot B)(p_{a},r_{b}):=c_{A}c_{B}\int\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mathrm{d}q_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{l}\mathrm{d}s_{j}I_{A}(p_{1},\dots,p_{m},q_{1},\dots,q_{k})I_{B}(r_{1},\dots,r_{n},s_{1},\dots,s_{l}).

This is relevant since some external variables
p_{a}
of the amplitude
A
might coincide with some integration variables
s_{j}
of
B
, i.e.,
p_{a}=s_{j}
for some
a\in\{1,\dots,n\}
and
j\in\{1,\dots,l\}
, and vice versa.
Accordingly, these are not external variables of the product
A\cdot B
.

To give an example of an amplitude, for
\Gamma
in equation (
2.3
) there is one external variable
p
for the external face and one integration variable
q
for the internal face leading to the amputated amplitude

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{}}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathrm{d}q\frac{1}{2|p|^{2\zeta}+\mu}\frac{1}{\big(|p|^{2\zeta}+|q|^{2\zeta}+\mu\big)^{2}}.

For
d\geq{2\zeta}
this integral does not converge.
To render the algebra of formal amplitudes
\mathcal{A}
an algebra of well defined functions it is necessary to introduce a regularization cutoff
\Lambda
, that is consider the algebra
\mathcal{A}^{\Lambda}
of the same integrals but
integrating all internal variables over the domain
|q|^{2\zeta}\leq\Lambda^{2\zeta}
,

\displaystyle A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma}(\{p_{f}\}):=\prod_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\Gamma}}\lambda_{\gamma_{v}}\prod_{f\in\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{int}}}\int_{\Lambda}\mathrm{d}q_{f}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}}\frac{1}{\sum_{a=1}^{r}|p_{i}^{a}|^{2\zeta}+\mu}.

(2.4)

For a well-defined limit
\Lambda\to\infty
renormalization is needed.

3
BPHZ renormalization using the Hopf algebra

of strand graphs

To renormalize a divergent amplitude one subtracts a counter term which exactly eliminates the divergent part and leaves a finite result.
To this end one needs a measure of how much a divergent amplitude is divergent.
A useful starting point is the power
\omega_{\Gamma}
of the asymptotic scaling in the cutoff
\Lambda
of the regularized amplitude (
2.4
), i.e.,
A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma}\sim\Lambda^{\omega_{\Gamma}}
.
A simple way to determine this quantity is to count the number of integrals and propagators in the integration variables in the amplitude.
For (
2.4
) this gives the
superficial degree of divergence

\displaystyle\omega^{\textrm{sd}}(\Gamma)=dF_{\Gamma}-{2\zeta}E_{\Gamma}+\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\Gamma}}\omega(\gamma_{v}),

(3.1)

where
F_{\Gamma}=|\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{int}}_{\Gamma}|
is the number of internal faces,
E_{\Gamma}=|\mathcal{E}_{\Gamma}|
is the number of (internal) edges and a scaling
\lambda_{\gamma}\sim\Lambda^{\omega(\gamma)}
of the couplings with vertex graph
\gamma=\gamma_{v}
for each vertex
v\in\mathcal{V}_{\Gamma}
in the strand graph
\Gamma
is assumed in addition.
A strand graph
\Gamma
is
superficially divergent
iff
\omega^{\textrm{sd}}(\Gamma)\geq 0
.
These properties are specific to a given combinatorially non-local field theory
T
which is defined by a set of interactions given by its vertex graphs
\mathbf{G}_{1}^{v}
together with their scaling weights
\omega\colon\mathbf{G}_{1}^{v}\to\mathbb{R}
, the propagators with scaling
{2\zeta}
and the dimension
d
.

The theorem of Bogoliubov and Parasiuk
[
7
]
with proof completed by Hepp
[
27
]
and further improvements by Zimmermann leading to the forest formula

[
55
]
states that in a renormalizable local quantum field theory all divergences can be renormalized by counter terms for each superficially divergent one-particle irreducible (1PI) diagram.
Kreimer
[
29
]
has further significantly improved the understanding of the combinatorics of the forest formula (in particular, and renormalization in much more general) showing that it has an algebraic structure given by a Hopf algebra of divergent Feynman diagrams.
In
[
53
]
I have shown that this Hopf algebra exists not only in field theories with point-like interactions but also for theories with any combinatorially non-local interactions,
in this way generalizing and improving similar statements for some specific examples
[
45
,
49
,
50
]
.
Here I demonstrate how this works explicitly using the BPHZ momentum scheme.

The challenge to define the right counter term to renormalize a divergent amplitude lies in the nested structure of divergent subdiagrams.
In cNLFT, just like in local quantum field theory
[
9
]
, a strand graph
\Theta
is a
subgraph

\Theta\subset\Gamma
of a strand graph
\Gamma
iff it has a subset of edges
\mathcal{E}_{\Theta}\subset\mathcal{E}_{\Gamma}
, including the adjacent strands, and the same structure otherwise
[
53
]
.
A
primitively divergent
strand graph is then one which has no proper subgraphs which are superficially divergent.
For a primitively divergent strand graph
\Gamma
one defines the renormalized amplitude
A_{\textsc{r}}(\Gamma)
directly by a subtraction operation which is a linear operator
R\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
as

\displaystyle A_{\textsc{r}}\colon\ \mathcal{G}\to A_{\textsc{r}}(\Gamma):=(A-R\circ A)(\Gamma).

(3.2)

The explicit form of
R
is exactly what specifies a particular renormalization scheme.
For concreteness, let us here define
R
for the BPHZ momentum scheme of cNLFT:

Definition 3.1

(BPHZ momentum scheme)
.

The operator
R\colon\mathcal{A}^{\Lambda}\to\mathcal{A}^{\Lambda}
on the unital commutative algebra
\mathcal{A}^{\Lambda}
of functions of the form
A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma}
, equation (
2.4
), with degree of divergence
\omega\big(A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma}\big):=\omega^{\textrm{sd}}(\Gamma)
, equation (
3.1
), is given by the multivariate Taylor expansion
T^{\omega}
of order
\omega=\omega\big(A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma}\big)
,

\displaystyle R\big[A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma}\big](\{p_{f}\}):=\big(T^{\omega}_{\{p_{f}\}}A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma}\big)(\{p_{f}\})=\sum_{|\vec{k}|\leq\omega(A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma})}\frac{1}{\vec{k}!}\frac{\partial^{|\vec{k}|}A_{\Gamma}^{\Lambda}}{\prod_{f}\partial p_{f}^{k_{f}}}\big(\{p_{f}=0\}\big)\prod_{f\in\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\Gamma}}p_{f}^{k_{f}},

(3.3)

where the sum is over multi-indices
\vec{k}
of length
|\vec{k}|=\sum_{f\in\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\Gamma}}k_{f}
.
Note that the underlying strand-graph structure is only used to encode the form of the function
A(\{p_{f}\})=A^{\Lambda}_{\Gamma}(\{p_{f}\})

but the definition of
R
is otherwise independent of it (any
\Lambda
-regularized integral has a degree
\omega
given by its scaling
\Lambda^{\omega}
).

For divergent diagrams
\Gamma
with subdivergences the whole counter term is a nested sum over counter terms for the various superficially divergent subgraphs according to Zimmermann’s forest formula
[
55
]
.
These terms are products of counter terms of subdiagrams
\Theta\subset\Gamma
and amplitudes of remaining diagrams in which the subdiagram is shrunken to a vertex, that is contractions
\Gamma/\Theta
.
For strand graphs
\Theta\subset\Gamma
the definition of such contraction
\Gamma/\Theta
is that there is a vertex for each connected component of
\Theta
and all internal edges and internal strands (and thus internal faces) of
\Theta
are deleted (see
[
53
, Definition 3.2]
for further detail).
This defines a coproduct
\Delta
on the algebra of superficially divergent strand graphs
\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}
of a given renormalizable theory
T
as

\displaystyle\Delta\colon\ \mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}\to\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}\otimes\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T},\qquad\Delta\Gamma:=\sum_{\Theta\subset\Gamma,\Theta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}}\Theta\otimes\Gamma/\Theta.

For this it is crucial that
\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}
is closed under contractions which is satisfied due to the property of renormalizability
\omega(\partial\Gamma)=\omega^{\textrm{sd}}(\Gamma)-\delta_{\Gamma}
where the
\Gamma
-dependent part
\delta_{\Gamma}
needs to satisfy
\delta_{\Gamma}=\delta_{\Theta}+\delta_{\Gamma/\Theta}
for all subgraphs
\Theta\subset\Gamma

[
53
]
.
Together with the counit
\epsilon\colon\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}\to\mathbb{Q}
defined as the projector to strand graphs without any edges,
\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}
is a coalgebra and due to compatibility with multiplication also a bialgebra
[
53
, Proposition 4.2]
.

To implement the forest formula, the crucial object is an inverse to the algebra homomorphism of amplitudes
A\colon\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}\to\mathcal{A}

with respect to the convolution product, i.e.,

\displaystyle\phi*\psi:=m_{\mathcal{A}}\circ(\phi\otimes\psi)\circ\Delta

for arbitrary such homomorphisms
\phi,\psi\colon\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}\to\mathcal{A}
.
Such inverse is a natural consequence if
\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}
is a Hopf algebra, i.e., has a
coinverse
, also called
antipode
,
S\colon\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}\to\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}
defined by
S*\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}*S=u\circ\epsilon
.
In fact, one can show that the bialgebra
\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}
of superficially divergent strand graphs in
T
is a Hopf algebra
[
53
, Theorem 5.1]
using the possibility to express
S
recursively as

\displaystyle S=-(S*P),

where
P=\mathrm{id}-u\circ\epsilon
is the projector to the augmentation ideal, i.e., all strand graphs in
\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}
with at least one edge
[
9
,
35
]
. This works because
\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}
is graded with respect to the number of edges.
As a direct consequence, the inverse of an algebra homomorphism
\phi
is
S^{\phi}=S\circ\phi
.
Both facts can now be used to recursively define the counter term

\displaystyle S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}\colon\

\displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}\to\mathcal{A},

(3.4)

\displaystyle S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}(\Gamma_{0})=1,\qquad S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}(\Gamma)=-R\big[\big(S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}*A\circ P\big)(\Gamma)\big]=-\sum_{\Theta\subsetneq\Gamma,\,\Theta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textrm{f2g}}_{T}}R\big[S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}(\Theta)A(\Gamma/\Theta)\big]

for any strand graph
\Gamma_{0}
without edges, and any
\Gamma
in the augmentation ideal.
Then, the renormalized amplitude is simply

\displaystyle\boxed{\phantom{\Big(}A_{\textsc{r}}:=S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}*A.\phantom{\Big)}}

The counter term map
S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}
is an algebra homomorphism, in particular
S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}(\Gamma_{1}\Gamma_{2})=S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}(\Gamma_{1})S^{\textsc{a}}_{\textsc{r}}(\Gamma_{2})
, if the subtraction map
R
is a Rota–Baxter operator, that is satisfies

\displaystyle R[AB]+R[A]R[B]=R[R[A]B+AR[B]].

Proposition 3.2
.

The BPHZ momentum subtraction operator
R=T^{\omega}

(
Definition
3.1
)
is a Rota–Baxter operator.

Proof.

The statement is equivalent to Proposition 9.1 in
[
19
]
.
There, the subtraction operator is defined on the integrands of the amplitudes which are ignorant about the degree
\omega
with the consequence that each specific
R
depends on
\omega
and it defines therefore a Rota–Baxter family (which still is very close to a Rota–Baxter operator by Proposition 9.2 therein).
As
R
is defined in Theorem
3.1
via the scaling
\Lambda^{\omega}
of
\Lambda
-regularized integrals,
this construction is not necessary.
4
4

4

I thank one of the referees for pointing out this subtlety.

∎

4
BPHZ renormalization in tensorial
\boldsymbol{\Phi^{4}_{2,2}}
and
\boldsymbol{\Phi^{4}_{1,3}}
theory

To demonstrate how BPHZ renormalization works, I give the example of tadpole and sunrise amplitudes in the just renormalizable complex tensorial field theories of rank
r=2
and
r=3
.
A tensorial
\Phi^{n}_{d,r}
theory is a cNLFT of a scalar field
\Phi
with
r
arguments in a
d
-dimensional manifold with tensor-invariant interactions of maximal order
n
(degree of the vertex)
[
2
]
.
An interaction is tensor-invariant if its vertex graph
\gamma
is
r
-regular and edge-coloured, i.e., each vertex in
\gamma
is adjacent to exactly
r
edges with distinct labels
c=1,2,\dots,r

[
8
]
.
This corresponds to fixing the position of each argument in the field and pairing only arguments in the same position.
As a consequence, also the strand graphs
\Gamma
labelling the perturbative expansion can be represented as coloured graphs,
5
5

5

Strictly speaking, this is only true for theories without multi-trace vertices, that is vertices whose vertex graphs have more than one connected component. Otherwise, the full coloured strand-graph structure is necessary
[
53
]
.

now with
r+1
colours.
In the following I will consider a complex field
\Phi
, just for the reason that the vertex graphs then have to be furthermore bipartite which simplifies the theory space further.
Thus, the action of such theory is

\displaystyle S[\Phi,\bar{\Phi}]=\left(\prod_{c=1}^{r}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathrm{d}p^{c}\right)\bar{\Phi}(\boldsymbol{p})\left(\sum_{c=1}^{r}|p^{c}|^{2\zeta}+\mu\right)\Phi(\boldsymbol{p})+\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbf{G}_{1}^{v}}\lambda_{\gamma}\operatorname{Tr}_{\gamma}\big(\Phi,\bar{\Phi}\big),

where
\operatorname{Tr}_{\gamma}
denotes the convolution of the field, detailed in equation (
2.1
), according to a given graph
\gamma
in the set
\mathbf{G}_{1}^{v}
of the theory’s interaction vertex graphs.

With weight
\omega(\gamma_{v})=d_{r}-{d^{v}}(d_{r}-{2\zeta})/2
for each
d^{v}
-valent vertex with vertex graph
\gamma_{v}
, the superficial degree of divergence in tensorial
\Phi^{n}_{d,r}
theory is
[
2
,
53
]

\displaystyle\omega^{\textrm{sd}}(\Gamma)=d_{r}-\frac{d_{r}-{2\zeta}}{2}V_{\partial\Gamma}-d\left(\frac{2\omega^{\textsc{g}}_{\Gamma}-2\omega^{\textsc{g}}_{\partial\Gamma}}{(r-1)!}+K_{\partial\Gamma}-1\right),

where
d_{r}=d(r-1)
is the equivalent of dimension compared to local field theory,
K_{\partial\Gamma}
is the number of connected components of the boundary graph and
\omega^{\textsc{g}}\in\mathbb{N}
is the Gurau degree of a coloured graph
[
25
,
26
]
.
It is a quantity generalizing the genus
g
in the
r=2
case, though not a topological invariant.
Crucially, the overall Gurau degree is conserved under the coproduct
[
45
]
such that renormalizability is given as
\omega^{\textrm{sd}}(\Gamma)=\omega(\partial\Gamma)-\delta_{\Gamma}
with
\delta_{\Gamma}=d\frac{2\omega^{\textsc{g}}_{\Gamma}-2\omega^{\textsc{g}}_{\partial\Gamma}}{(r-1)!}
.
One can further show that
\omega^{\textsc{g}}_{\Gamma}\geq\omega^{\textsc{g}}_{\partial\Gamma}

[
3
]

such that the whole term in brackets is always greater or equal to zero and renormalizable theories are determined by the first two terms.
Thus, a tensorial
\Phi^{n}_{d,r}
theory is just renormalizable if
n=\frac{2d_{r}}{d_{r}-{2\zeta}}
.

Just-renormalizable quartic theories are those with
d_{r}=d(r-1)=4\zeta
.
The tensorial equivalent to standard local
\phi^{4}_{4}
theory with quadratic propagator
\zeta=1
are therefore theories with
d_{r}=4
, that is theories with
(d,r)=(4,2),(2,3)
or
(1,5)
. Let us here simplify explicit renormalization even further and chose
\zeta=1/2
. The two just renormalizable theories are then tensorial
\Phi^{4}_{2,2}
and
\Phi^{4}_{1,3}
theory.
The divergence degree in these two theories is

\displaystyle\omega^{\textrm{sd}}(\Gamma)=dF-E=2-\frac{1}{2}V_{\partial\Gamma}-\begin{cases}2\left(2g_{\Gamma}+K_{\partial\Gamma}-1\right)&\textrm{for $\Phi^{4}_{2,2}$ theory},\\
\left(\omega^{\textsc{g}}_{\Gamma}-g_{\partial\Gamma}+K_{\partial\Gamma}-1\right)&\textrm{for $\Phi^{4}_{1,3}$ theory}.\end{cases}

In both cases there is only a single type of marginal quartic interaction given by the graph
and
c
for
c=1,2,3
respectively.
It is not necessary to include the quartic double-trace interaction.

For these two cases I will present the explicit BPHZ-renormalized amplitudes
A_{\Gamma}
for the tadpole and sunrise diagrams.
Complex
\Phi^{4}_{2,2}
theory is very similar to the quartic Hermitian matrix field theory known as the Grosse-Wulkenhaar model or quartic Kontsevich model
[
23
,
28
,
54
]
, i.e., has the same power counting and the same set of divergent diagrams with identical amplitudes;
for this theory I simply reproduce known results
[
28
]
with the Hopf algebra method.
The rank
r=3
tensorial theory is one of the first for which renormalizability was proven
[
4
]
.
In this case the calculations presented here are new explicit results of amplitudes in tensorial field theory.

The tadpole in
\boldsymbol{\Phi^{4}_{2,2}}
theory

The only primitive 2-point amplitude in
\Phi^{4}_{2,2}
theory is the one for the tadpole strand graph.

\displaystyle\hphantom{A_{r}(p_1,p_2,p_3)=}{}-\log(\tilde{p}_{1})(\tilde{p}_{1}+1)\log(\tilde{p}_{1}+1)+\tilde{p}_{23}\Big(\textrm{Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{1}{\tilde{p}_{23}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log^{2}(\tilde{p}_{23})+2\zeta_{2}\Big)

(4.5)

where again
\tilde{p}_{1}=|p_{1}|/\mu
and
\tilde{p}_{23}=(|p_{2}|+|p_{3}|)/\mu
.
Note that the Taylor operator
T^{0}_{p_{1},p_{2},p_{3}}
in the first line acts on the whole expression which is following.
One might use shuffle relations of multiple polylogarithms to further simplify the terms of weight two in
\tilde{p}_{1}+1
and
\tilde{p}_{23}
.

Interestingly, the calculation of the sunrise diagram in the
r=3
theory is simpler than in the
r=2
case due to the lack of overlapping divergences.
This is an instance of the well known breaking of the combinatorial symmetry of matrix field theory which
xleads to asymptotic freedom in quartic tensorial field theories
[
47
]
.
In general, the expectation is that amplitudes in tensorial field theory can always be expanded in multiple polylogarithms for which efficient algorithms exist for computation
[
40
]
.

5
Outlook

The main purpose of this contribution has been to demonstrate how the Connes–Kreimer Hopf algebra
[
16
,
17
,
29
,
30
]
can be used for explicit calculations in cNLFT.
Feynman diagrams in cNLFT are strand graphs generalizing the usual Feynman graphs of point-like interactions by adding a second layer of strands along which the degrees of freedom in cNLFT propagate.
The crucial difference to standard quantum field theory is that the external structure of such diagrams is not just given by the number of legs of a given field type but is captured by graphs.
Nevertheless, with the right definitions, the Hopf-algebraic structure relying on the usual coproduct of subgraph contraction is exactly the same as for local quantum field theory
[
53
]
.
Thus, it directly gives a convenient algorithm to renormalize Green’s functions in cNLFT, such as non-commutative field theory and matrix field theory
[
23
,
28
,
54
]
as well as higher rank tensorial and group field theories
[
2
,
3
,
13
,
20
,
37
]
.

While the Hopf algebra unveils the structure of renormalization independent of a specific scheme, here I have demonstrated how it works for BPHZ momentum subtraction
[
7
,
27
,
55
]
in two simple examples of tensorial field theory on
\big(\mathbb{R}^{d}\big)^{\otimes r}
.
As a first example, in
\Phi^{4}_{2,2}
theory, i.e., complex matrix field theory on a 2-dimensional configuration space, the tadpole and sunrise diagram have the same amplitude as in the Grosse–Wulkenhaar model
[
23
,
54
]
and the Hopf-algebraic calculations reproduce the known results
[
28
]
.
Second, as a first example of a field theory of higher rank
r>2
, I have calculated the amplitudes for the same diagrams in
\Phi^{4}_{1,3}
theory.
As to be expected, these calculations give first hints that also in tensorial field theories the algebra of amplitudes is spanned by multiple polylogarithms.
A deeper understanding of this space of amplitudes for tensorial theories would be an interesting research topic in its own.

The renormalized amplitudes of the tensorial versions of the tadpole and sunrise diagrams give examples showing that the UV regime of tensorial field theories
[
2
]
is richer than the large-
N
limit of the corresponding tensor models
[
25
,
26
]
.
The latter is completely described by so-called melonic diagrams, i.e., diagrams which have vanishing Gurau degree
\omega^{\textsc{g}}=0
.
There have been considerable efforts to find random geometries beyond the melonic regime, for example by enhancement of subleading classes of diagrams
[
18
,
33
,
34
]
.
In tensorial field theories, melonic diagrams are the most divergent but not the only divergent ones.
In fact, the tadpole and sunrise amplitudes (
4.2
) and (
4.5
) are examples of divergent, non-melonic amplitudes.
Thus, in renormalized quantities they contribute as much as the melonic contributions.
Such effects make tensorial field theory an interesting candidate to find new regimes of the theory beyond the melonic one.
